engine: markdown
title: "rush convert"
---

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'mtcars'
```

The `convert` command converts files between [formats](../formats.qmd)
without an R expression. It reads the input, and writes it in the format of
the output file's extension, or of `--output-format` (`-O`).

## Usage

```bash
rush convert [options] [<file>...]
```

## Converting a file

Name the output file with `--output` (`-o`):

```{term}
rush convert -o mtcars.parquet mtcars.csv
rush run 'nrow(df)' mtcars.parquet
```

Or write to standard output with `-O`:

```{term}
rush convert -O jsonl --head 2 mtcars.csv
```

Converting to a format that `rush` can only read, such as `.xls`, is an
error.

## Multiple files with output templates

To convert multiple files to separate files, give the output a template with
yt-dlp-style placeholders. Each input gets its own output file. (To combine
them in one file instead, write a [database or spreadsheet](#database-and-spreadsheet-output).)

```{term}
printf 'id,val\n1,a\n2,b\n' > chunk1.csv
printf 'id,val\n3,c\n4,d\n' > chunk2.csv
rush convert -o '%(file_name)s.parquet' chunk1.csv chunk2.csv
ls chunk*
```

| Placeholder | Description |
|-------------|-------------|
| `%(file_name)s` | Input file name, without its extension |
| `%(file_index)d` | 1-based position of the input file |
| `%(table_name)s` | Table name (databases) |
| `%(table_index)d` | 1-based position of the table (databases) |

The format after the `)` follows `sprintf()`: `s` for text, `d` for a
number, `03d` for a number padded with zeros. Use `l` or `u` for text in
lowercase or uppercase. For example, to write every table of a database to
its own file:

```{term}
#| include: false
rush convert -o garage.duckdb chunk1.csv chunk2.csv
```

```{term}
rush convert -o 'table_%(table_index)02d_%(table_name)s.csv' garage.duckdb
ls table_*
```

## Database and spreadsheet output

When the output is a database (DuckDB or SQLite), each input becomes a
table, named after the input file:

```{term}
rush convert -o chunks.duckdb chunk1.csv chunk2.csv
rush run 'names(dfs$chunks)' chunks.duckdb
```

A spreadsheet (Excel or ODS) works the same way, with a sheet per input:

```{term}
rush convert -o chunks.xlsx chunk1.csv chunk2.csv
rush run -l readxl 'excel_sheets("chunks.xlsx")'
```

Converting a database to another database copies all its tables, and
converting it to a spreadsheet gives a sheet per table:

```{term}
rush convert -o chunks.sqlite chunks.duckdb
rush run 'names(dfs$chunks)' chunks.sqlite
rush convert -o tables.xlsx chunks.duckdb
rush run -l readxl 'excel_sheets("tables.xlsx")'
```

## Options

### `--head`

Write only the first rows:

```{term}
rush convert --head 3 -o top3.csv mtcars.csv
cat top3.csv
```

### `--input-format` (`-F`), `--output-format` (`-O`)

Choose the formats regardless of the extensions:

```{term}
cp mtcars.csv mtcars.dat
rush convert -F csv -O json --head 2 mtcars.dat
```

### Format-specific options

The options that set delimiters, headers, sheets, indentation, and element
names work as in [`rush run`](run.qmd#format-specific-options). For example,
`--output-delimiter` (`-D`):

```{term}
rush convert -D ';' --head 3 -o semicolons.csv mtcars.csv
cat semicolons.csv
```

## Help

```{term}
rush convert -h
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f mtcars.csv mtcars.parquet mtcars.dat chunk1.csv chunk2.csv
rm -f chunk1.parquet chunk2.parquet garage.duckdb table_*.csv
rm -f chunks.duckdb chunks.sqlite chunks.xlsx tables.xlsx top3.csv semicolons.csv
```
